quotes.text: Breaking into a network is hard, and logging in with a stolen password is easy. Microsoft puts it bluntly when it says that adversaries aren't breaking in, they're signing in.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains in one line why identity has become the main attack surface.

quotes.text: A risky sign in is usually handled right there with the second check. While a risky account often needs a password change because the password itself may already be out there.

quotes.why: Makes the difference between sign-in risk and user risk practical by tying each to its fix.

quotes.text: Conditional access itself comes with P1, but the risk based version of it needs P2. That single distinction explains most of the confusion.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters

chapters.title: Two kinds of risk: user and sign-in
How risk turns into a decision
What it costs and what you need

takeaways: Microsoft Entra ID Protection scores every sign-in and every account as low, medium or high risk, separating sign-in risk from user risk.
Conditional Access turns those scores into decisions, so users can self-remediate with MFA or a secure password change while admins handle what remains.
Risk-based policies need Entra ID P2, and safe rollout means MFA registration first, excluded break-glass accounts, trusted locations and report-only mode.
hook: Most identity attacks are simply password attacks, and a leaked password is the usual way into a Microsoft 365 account. This Simply Explained episode is for admins and security beginners who want to understand how Microsoft Entra ID Protection scores sign-in and user risk, hands it to Conditional Access, lets users fix risk themselves, and which licenses and best practices you need.
